---
title: Glossary
guide-section: "Reference"
---

This page defines the terms used throughout the EdgeCase documentation, in alphabetical order. Most
are standard terms of graph theory and network science; a few are specific to EdgeCase, such as
**node ID**, **selection**, and **step log**. Where a term has a counterpart in EdgeCase's API, the
relevant class, method, or function is shown in `code`. Terms in **bold** have their own entry on
this page, and each "Learn more" link leads to the page of this guide that covers the term in
depth.

A\* search
: A **shortest path** algorithm that steers its search toward the target with a *heuristic*, an
  estimate of the remaining distance from each node, such as the straight-line distance between two
  places on a map. With a heuristic that never overestimates, A* finds the same path as **Dijkstra's
  algorithm** while exploring far fewer nodes. Available via `astar_path()` and
  `astar_path_length()`, with `alt_heuristic()` building a heuristic from landmark distances. [Learn
  more](paths.qmd#a-search).

Adamic–Adar index
: A **link prediction** score for a pair of nodes that counts their **common neighbors**, giving
  each one a weight of $1 / \log k$, where $k$ is its **degree**. A shared friend with few other
  friends says more about a pair than a shared celebrity. Available via `adamic_adar_index()`. See
  also **resource allocation index**. [Learn more](similarity.qmd#link-prediction).

Adjacency list
: A representation of a graph that lists, for each node, the nodes it links to. It is compact for
  **sparse graphs** and is a common plain-text file format. Available via `to_adjlist()` and
  `from_adjlist()`. [Learn more](file-formats.qmd#adjacency-lists).

Adjacency matrix
: A square matrix $A$ with one row and one column per node, in which $A_{ij}$ is the **weight** of
  the edge from node $i$ to node $j$ (1 in an unweighted graph) and 0 where there is no edge. An
  **undirected graph** has a symmetric adjacency matrix. Matrix products of $A$ count **walks**: the
  entries of $A^k$ count the walks of $k$ steps. Available via `adjacency_matrix()`,
  `to_numpy_array()`, and `to_scipy_sparse_array()`, and read back with `from_numpy_array()` and
  `from_scipy_sparse_array()`. See also **Laplacian matrix** and **spectrum**. [Learn
  more](spectral.qmd#the-adjacency-matrix).

Algebraic connectivity
: The second-smallest eigenvalue of the **Laplacian matrix**. It is 0 exactly when the graph is
  disconnected, and larger values mean a graph that is harder to cut into pieces. The eigenvector
  that belongs to it is the **Fiedler vector**. Available via `algebraic_connectivity()`. [Learn
  more](connectivity.qmd#algebraic-connectivity).

Ancestor
: In a **directed graph**, a node from which a given node can be reached along directed edges. The
  nodes reachable *from* a node are its **descendants**. In a **DAG** of tasks, the ancestors of a
  task are everything that must be done before it. Available via `ancestors()` and `descendants()`.
  See also **lowest common ancestor**. [Learn more](dags.qmd#ancestors-and-descendants).

Antichain
: A set of nodes in a **DAG** of which no node is an **ancestor** of another, so that none of them
  has to wait for the others. The largest antichain measures how much of the work can proceed in
  parallel. Available via `antichains()` and `antichain_width()`. [Learn
  more](dags.qmd#antichains).

Arborescence
: A **directed graph** that is a **tree** with all edges pointing away from a single root, so that
  every other node has exactly one incoming edge. A *branching* is a collection of arborescences.
  Available via `is_arborescence()`, `is_branching()`, and `minimum_spanning_arborescence()`. See
  also **spanning tree**. [Learn more](dags.qmd#trees).

Articulation point
: A node whose removal disconnects the graph, or more generally increases its number of
  **components**. Also called a *cut vertex*. A graph without articulation points is *biconnected*.
  Available via `articulation_points()`, with the biconnected pieces from
  `biconnected_components()`. See also **bridge**. [Learn more](connectivity.qmd#weak-points).

Assortativity
: The tendency of nodes to link to nodes that are similar to them. *Degree assortativity* is the
  correlation between the **degrees** at the two ends of the edges: positive when hubs link to hubs,
  as in many social networks, and negative when hubs link to poorly connected nodes, as in many
  technological and biological networks. Assortativity by a categorical **attribute** measures
  **homophily**. Available via `assortativity_degree()`, `assortativity()` for numeric
  attributes, and `assortativity_nominal()` for categories. See also **mixing matrix**. [Learn
  more](structure.qmd#mixing-patterns).

Attribute
: A named value stored on a node or an edge, such as an age, a category, or a score. Each attribute
  is a column of the **node table** or the **edge table**. Attributes are set with `add_node()` and
  `add_edge()` keyword arguments, `set_node_attrs()`, and `set_edge_attrs()`, and read with
  `get_node_attrs()` and `get_edge_attrs()`. Most analysis methods also write their results to an
  attribute (see **stored results**). Two attributes are special: the node **type** and the edge
  **rel**. [Learn more](node-and-edge-data.qmd).

Automorphism
: An **isomorphism** of a graph with itself: a relabelling of the nodes that preserves every edge.
  The automorphisms describe a graph's symmetries, and nodes that some automorphism maps onto each
  other are structurally indistinguishable. Available via `automorphism_cosets()` and
  `canonical_labeling()`. [Learn more](similarity.qmd#symmetries).

Average degree
: The mean **degree** of the nodes, $2m / n$ for an undirected graph with $n$ nodes and $m$ edges.
  In a directed graph, the mean in-degree and the mean out-degree are both $m / n$. Available via
  `average_degree()`. See also **density**. [Learn more](structure.qmd#degrees).

Barabási–Albert model
: See **preferential attachment**.

Benchmark graph
: A random graph generated with known communities, used to test **community detection** methods,
  since the right answer is known. The *planted partition* model gives groups of equal size, and the
  *LFR benchmark* gives heterogeneous degrees and community sizes, as in real networks. Available
  via `add_planted_partition_graph()` and `add_lfr_graph()`. See also **stochastic block model**.
  [Learn more](generators.qmd#community-benchmarks).

Betweenness centrality
: A **centrality** that scores a node by the share of **shortest paths** between other pairs of
  nodes that pass through it. Nodes with high betweenness are brokers and bottlenecks, which link
  parts of the network that would otherwise be far apart. *Edge betweenness* scores edges in the
  same way. Available via `betweenness_centrality()` and `edge_betweenness_centrality()`, with group
  and subset variants. See also **Girvan–Newman method**. [Learn
  more](centrality.qmd#betweenness-centrality).

Bipartite graph
: A graph whose nodes divide into two sets, with every edge joining a node of one set to a node of
  the other: people and the events they attend, or genes and the diseases they are linked to. Also
  called *two-mode* data. A graph is bipartite exactly when it has no **cycle** of odd length.
  EdgeCase marks the two sides with a `bipartite` attribute of 0 and 1, as NetworkX does. Available
  via `is_bipartite()`, `bipartite_sets()`, `from_biadjacency_matrix()`, and `layout_bipartite()`.
  See also **projection**. [Learn more](other-libraries.qmd#two-mode-data).

Bond percolation
: See **percolation**.

Breadth-first search (BFS)
: A **traversal** that visits a start node, then all of its neighbors, then all of their unvisited
  neighbors, and so on, so that nodes are reached in order of their distance in steps. It finds
  **shortest paths** in unweighted graphs. Available via `bfs()`, `bfs_edges()`, `bfs_layers()`, and
  `bfs_tree()`. See also **depth-first search**. [Learn more](traversals.qmd#searching).

Bridge
: An edge whose removal disconnects the graph, or increases its number of **components**. A *local
  bridge* is an edge whose endpoints have no **common neighbors**, so that removing it makes them
  far apart without necessarily disconnecting them; local bridges are the "weak ties" that link
  separate groups. Available via `bridges()`, `has_bridges()`, and `local_bridges()`. See also
  **articulation point**. [Learn more](connectivity.qmd#weak-points).

Brokerage
: A node's position between others who are not themselves linked, which lets it pass on, or
  withhold, what flows between them. Burt's measures of *structural holes* quantify it: the
  *constraint* of a node is high when its contacts are all linked to each other, and its *effective
  size* counts its non-redundant contacts. Available via `constraint()`, `local_constraint()`, and
  `effective_size()`. See also **betweenness centrality**. [Learn
  more](centrality.qmd#brokerage).

Center
: The nodes of smallest **eccentricity**, which are the closest to all others in the worst case. The
  *periphery* is the nodes of largest eccentricity. Available via `center()` and
  `periphery()`, with `barycenter()` for the nodes of smallest total distance. See also
  **radius** and **diameter**. [Learn more](structure.qmd#distances).

Centrality
: Any measure of how important or prominent a node is, judged by its position in the network. Each
  measure formalizes a different idea of importance: having many ties (**degree centrality**), being
  close to everyone (**closeness centrality**), lying between others (**betweenness centrality**),
  or being linked to other important nodes (**eigenvector centrality**, **PageRank**). EdgeCase's
  centrality methods store their scores in a node attribute named after the method, or return them
  with `return_dict=True` (see **stored results**), and `select_nodes_by_centrality()` selects the
  most central nodes. [Learn more](centrality.qmd).

Chaining
: Writing several method calls one after another in a single expression, such as
  `ec.karate_club().pagerank().cmty_louvain()`. Methods that build, change, or annotate a graph
  return the graph itself, so a sequence of steps reads as a pipeline from top to bottom. Methods
  that answer a question, such as `count_nodes()`, return the answer instead, and end a chain.
  [Learn more](get-started.qmd#three-ideas-that-run-through-the-library).

Chordal graph
: A graph in which every **cycle** of four or more nodes has a *chord*, an edge joining two nodes
  that are not next to each other on the cycle. Chordal graphs have efficient algorithms for
  problems that are hard in general, such as **coloring** and finding the largest **clique**.
  Available via `is_chordal()`, `chordal_graph_cliques()`, and `complete_to_chordal_graph()`. See
  also **treewidth**. [Learn more](coloring-matching.qmd#chordal-graphs-and-treewidth).

Clique
: A set of nodes in which every pair is linked. A *maximal* clique can't be extended by another
  node, and a *maximum* clique is a largest one; its size is the graph's *clique number*. Cliques
  are the tightest possible groups, though in real networks they are usually small and overlap
  heavily. Available via `find_cliques()`, `maximum_clique()`, `clique_number()`, and
  `node_clique_number()`. See also **k-core** and **k-truss**. [Learn
  more](structure.qmd#cliques).

Closeness centrality
: A **centrality** that scores a node by how near it is to all others: the reciprocal of its mean
  **distance** to the nodes it can reach. Nodes with high closeness can reach the rest of the
  network quickly. Available via `closeness_centrality()`. See also **harmonic centrality**. [Learn
  more](centrality.qmd#closeness-and-harmonic-centrality).

Clustering coefficient
: A measure of how much the neighbors of a node are linked to each other. A node's *local*
  clustering coefficient is the share of the pairs of its neighbors that are linked,
  $2T / (k(k - 1))$ for a node of **degree** $k$ in $T$ **triangles**. The *average* clustering
  coefficient is the mean over the nodes, and **transitivity** is a related global measure. High
  clustering, far above that of a **random graph**, is a hallmark of social networks. Available via
  `clustering_coefficient()`, `local_clustering_coefficient()`, and
  `average_clustering_coefficient()`. [Learn
  more](clustering-and-motifs.qmd#clustering-coefficients).

Co-expression network
: A network of genes in which two genes are linked when their expression levels rise and fall
  together across samples. The links are usually derived from correlations, either by keeping the
  strong ones or, in *WGCNA* (weighted gene co-expression network analysis), by raising every
  correlation to a power (see **soft thresholding**). Groups of co-expressed genes are found with
  **topological overlap** and **community detection**. [Learn
  more](network-biology.qmd#co-expression-networks).

Coloring
: An assignment of colors to the nodes so that no two linked nodes share a color. The fewest colors
  possible is the graph's *chromatic number*. Coloring models scheduling and allocation problems in
  which linked items conflict, such as exams that share students. An *edge coloring* colors the
  edges so that no two edges at a node share a color. Available via `greedy_color()`,
  `is_valid_coloring()`, `chromatic_number_upper_bound()`, and `edge_coloring()`. [Learn
  more](coloring-matching.qmd#coloring).

Common neighbors
: The nodes linked to both nodes of a pair. Their number is the simplest **similarity** of two nodes
  and the simplest **link prediction** score. Available via `get_common_neighbors()` and
  `common_neighbors()`. See also **Jaccard similarity** and **Adamic–Adar index**. [Learn
  more](similarity.qmd#neighborhood-similarity).

Community
: A group of nodes that are more densely linked to each other than to the rest of the network:
  circles of friends, research fields, functional modules of proteins. There is no single
  definition, and different **community detection** methods formalize the idea differently. A set of
  communities that places every node in exactly one is a **partition**. See also **modularity** and
  **conductance**. [Learn more](communities.qmd).

Community detection
: Finding the **communities** of a network from its edges alone. EdgeCase's methods share the prefix
  `cmty_`, such as `cmty_louvain()`, `cmty_leiden()`, `cmty_walktrap()`, and
  `cmty_label_propagation()`, and store each node's community number in an attribute named after the
  method. See also **Louvain method**, **Leiden method**, **label propagation**, **resolution**, and
  **stochastic block model**. [Learn more](communities.qmd).

Complement
: The graph on the same nodes that has an edge exactly where the original has none. Available via
  `complement()`. [Learn more](transforming.qmd#derived-graphs).

Complete graph
: A graph in which every pair of nodes is linked. The complete graph on $n$ nodes, $K_n$, has
  $n(n - 1)/2$ edges and a **density** of 1. Available via `add_full_graph()`. See also **clique**.

Component
: A maximal set of nodes that are all reachable from one another. A *connected* graph has a single
  component. In a **directed graph**, a **strongly connected component** requires paths in both
  directions, and a **weakly connected component** ignores edge directions. Available via
  `weakly_connected_components()`, `node_connected_component()`, `is_connected()`, and
  `largest_component_size()`. See also **giant component**. [Learn
  more](connectivity.qmd#connected-components).

Condensation
: The **DAG** formed by collapsing each **strongly connected component** of a directed graph into a
  single node. It shows the order in which the components can be reached. Available via
  `condensation()`. [Learn more](connectivity.qmd#directed-graphs).

Conductance
: A score for a single **community**: the number of edges leaving it divided by the total **degree**
  of its smaller side, so that a well-separated community has a low conductance. Available via
  `conductance()`, with the related `cut_size()`, `normalized_cut_size()`, and `volume()`. See also
  **modularity**. [Learn more](communities.qmd#scoring-single-communities).

Configuration model
: A **random graph** model that takes a **degree** sequence and links the nodes at random while
  giving each node exactly its prescribed degree. It is the standard **null model** for asking which
  properties of a network follow from its degrees alone. Available via `configuration_model()`, with
  `add_havel_hakimi_graph()` for a deterministic graph with given degrees. See also **rewiring**.
  [Learn more](generators.qmd#degree-sequences).

Connectivity
: The number of nodes (*node connectivity*) or edges (*edge connectivity*) that must be removed to
  disconnect a graph, or to separate two given nodes. By Menger's theorem, it equals the number of
  **disjoint paths** between them. A graph is *k-connected* when no fewer than $k$ removals
  disconnect it. Available via `node_connectivity()`, `edge_connectivity()`,
  `node_connectivity_between()`, and `k_components()`. See also **minimum cut**. [Learn
  more](connectivity.qmd#measuring-connectivity).

Coreness
: The largest $k$ for which a node belongs to the **k-core**. Nodes of high coreness sit in the
  dense center of a network, and coreness is often a better guide to a node's influence on
  **spreading** than its **degree**. Available via `coreness()`. [Learn
  more](structure.qmd#cores-and-dense-regions).

Critical path
: The longest path through a **DAG** of tasks weighted by their durations. It sets the shortest time
  in which the whole project can finish, and a delay to any task on it delays the project. Available
  via `dag_longest_path()` and `dag_longest_path_length()`. [Learn
  more](dags.qmd#the-critical-path).

Cycle
: A **path** that returns to its start without repeating any other node. A graph without cycles is
  *acyclic*: a **forest** if undirected, a **DAG** if directed. The length of the shortest cycle is
  the graph's **girth**. Available via `has_cycles()`, `simple_cycles()`, and `cycle_basis()`.
  [Learn more](clustering-and-motifs.qmd#cycles).

Cypher
: The query language of the Neo4j graph database and the openCypher standard, which describes the
  shapes to find in a graph as ASCII-art *patterns*, such as `(a:Person)-[:KNOWS]->(b)`. EdgeCase
  implements a subset of it, with `MATCH`, `WHERE`, `WITH`, `RETURN`, aggregation, `ORDER BY`,
  `SKIP`, and `LIMIT`. A node's **type** is read as its Cypher label and an edge's **rel** as its
  relationship type. Available via `match()`, which returns the matches as a Polars DataFrame,
  `count_matches()`, and `select_match()`, which turns the matches into a **selection**; graphs are
  exchanged with Cypher databases via `to_cypher()` and `from_cypher()`. [Learn
  more](cypher.qmd).

d-separation
: A criterion for reading conditional independence off a causal **DAG**: two sets of variables are
  d-separated by a third when every path between them is blocked by it. It tells which variables
  must be adjusted for to estimate a causal effect. Available via `is_d_separator()`,
  `find_minimal_d_separator()`, and `moral_graph()`. [Learn
  more](dags.qmd#causal-diagrams-and-d-separation).

DAG
: A *directed acyclic graph*, a **directed graph** without **cycles**. DAGs describe dependencies,
  such as tasks and their prerequisites, packages and their requirements, or causes and their
  effects, and their nodes can always be put in a **topological sort** order. Available via
  `is_dag()`. See also **critical path**, **ancestor**, and **transitive reduction**. [Learn
  more](dags.qmd).

Dataset
: One of the real-world networks that ship with EdgeCase or that it downloads on demand, from
  classics such as the karate club to networks with millions of edges. Each has a loader function,
  such as `karate_club()` or `power_grid()`, and the networks distributed as data files are also
  listed in a *registry*, used with `list_registered_datasets()`, `get_dataset_info()`, and
  `load_dataset()`. [Learn more](datasets.qmd).

Degree
: The number of edges at a node. In a **directed graph**, the *in-degree* counts incoming edges and
  the *out-degree* outgoing ones. In a **weighted graph**, the sum of the weights of a node's edges
  is its *strength*, or weighted degree. A **self-loop** adds 2 to the degree of its node. The node
  table always ends with a `degree` column. Available via `get_degree()`, `get_in_degree()`,
  `get_out_degree()`, and `degrees()`. [Learn more](structure.qmd#degrees).

Degree centrality
: A **centrality** that scores a node by its **degree**, divided by the largest possible degree,
  $n - 1$. It measures direct influence or activity. Available via `degree_centrality()`. [Learn
  more](centrality.qmd#degree-centrality).

Degree distribution
: The share of nodes with each **degree**. Many real networks have *heavy-tailed* degree
  distributions, in which most nodes have few ties and a few **hubs** have very many; this shapes
  their **robustness** and their **spreading** processes. Available via `degree_distribution()`.
  See also **scale-free network**. [Learn more](structure.qmd#degrees).

Density
: The share of the possible edges that are present: $2m / (n(n - 1))$ for an undirected graph with
  $n$ nodes and $m$ edges, and $m / (n(n - 1))$ for a directed one. Real networks are almost always
  *sparse*, with a density far below 1, and their density falls as they grow. Available via
  `density()`. [Learn more](structure.qmd#the-graph-at-a-glance).

Depth-first search (DFS)
: A **traversal** that follows one path as far as it goes before backing up to try the next. It
  underlies algorithms for **cycles**, **topological sorts**, and **articulation points**. Available
  via `dfs()`, `dfs_edges()`, `dfs_tree()`, and `dfs_postorder_nodes()`. See also **breadth-first
  search**. [Learn more](traversals.qmd#searching).

Descendant
: See **ancestor**.

Diameter
: The largest **distance** between any two nodes of a connected graph, which is also the largest
  **eccentricity**. Real networks have small diameters even when they are very large (see **small
  world**). Available via `diameter()`. See also **radius** and **mean distance**. [Learn
  more](structure.qmd#distances).

Differential network
: A comparison of two networks of the same nodes, such as the gene networks of healthy and diseased
  tissue, that finds the edges present in one condition and absent in the other. Available via
  `differential_edges()` and `edge_overlap()`. See also **graph edit distance**. [Learn
  more](network-biology.qmd#differential-networks).

Dijkstra's algorithm
: The standard algorithm for **shortest paths** in a **weighted graph** with non-negative weights.
  It settles the nodes in order of their distance from the source. Graphs with negative weights need
  the Bellman–Ford algorithm instead. EdgeCase's `shortest_path()` uses Dijkstra's algorithm on
  weighted graphs and **breadth-first search** on unweighted ones, while `bidirectional_dijkstra()`
  and `bellman_ford_shortest_path()` choose an algorithm explicitly. [Learn
  more](paths.qmd#choosing-an-algorithm).

Directed graph
: A graph whose edges have a direction, from a **source** node to a **target** node, as in
  citations, web links, or the flow of money. Also called a *digraph*. A graph is created as
  directed with `ec.Graph(directed=True)` and checked with `is_directed()`; `to_directed()`,
  `to_undirected()`, and `reverse()` change the direction of a graph's edges. See also **undirected
  graph** and **reciprocity**. [Learn more](graph-model.qmd#directed-and-undirected-graphs).

Disease module
: A connected region of a molecular interaction network that holds the genes associated with a
  disease. Disease genes tend to cluster in the network, so the module can be grown from a few known
  genes, or found by connecting the genes with high association scores. Available via
  `expand_seed_set()` and `prize_collecting_steiner_tree()`. See also **network propagation** and
  **enrichment**. [Learn more](network-biology.qmd#disease-modules).

Disjoint paths
: Paths between the same two nodes that share no edges (*edge-disjoint*) or no intermediate nodes
  (*node-disjoint*). Their number measures how many independent routes connect the nodes, and equals
  the **connectivity** between them. Available via `edge_disjoint_paths()` and
  `node_disjoint_paths()`. [Learn more](paths.qmd#disjoint-paths).

Distance
: The length of a **shortest path** between two nodes: the number of edges in an unweighted graph,
  or the sum of the edge **weights** in a weighted one. Nodes in different **components** are at
  infinite distance. Available via `shortest_path_length()`, `all_pairs_shortest_path_length()`, and
  `floyd_warshall()`. See also **eccentricity**, **mean distance**, and **resistance distance**.
  [Learn more](paths.qmd).

Dominating set
: A set of nodes such that every other node is linked to at least one of them, as when choosing
  sites for services that every neighborhood must be next to. Available via `dominating_set()`,
  `minimum_weighted_dominating_set()`, and `is_dominating_set()`. [Learn
  more](coloring-matching.qmd#dominating-sets).

Dominator
: In a directed graph with an entry node, a node $d$ *dominates* a node $v$ when every path from the
  entry to $v$ passes through $d$. Dominators are the unavoidable checkpoints of a control-flow
  graph or a supply chain. Available via `immediate_dominators()` and `dominance_frontiers()`.
  [Learn more](dags.qmd#dominators).

Eccentricity
: The largest **distance** from a node to any other node. The graph's **radius** is the smallest
  eccentricity and its **diameter** the largest. Available via `eccentricity()`. See also
  **center**. [Learn more](structure.qmd#distances).

Edge
: A link between two nodes, joining a **source** to a **target**. Also called a *link*, *tie*, *arc*
  (when directed), or *relationship*. Every edge in EdgeCase has an **edge ID**, a **rel**, an
  optional **weight**, and any number of **attributes**. Edges are added with `add_edge()` and
  `add_edges()`, and fetched as `Edge` objects with `get_edge()`. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#edges).

Edge ID
: The integer that EdgeCase assigns to each edge, starting from 1 in the order the edges are added.
  Edge IDs tell **parallel edges** apart, which share their endpoints. Available via
  `get_edge_ids()` and `find_edge_ids()`, which finds the IDs of the edges between two nodes, and
  used by `get_edge()`, `get_edge_attrs_by_id()`, `select_edges_by_id()`, and `delete_edge_by_id()`.
  See also **node ID**. [Learn more](graph-model.qmd#edges).

Edge list
: A table or file with one row per edge, giving its two endpoints and possibly its weight and other
  attributes. It is the most common way that network data arrives. Available via
  `Graph.from_edges()`, `from_pandas_edgelist()`, `from_tsv_edge_list()`, and
  `to_pandas_edgelist()`, and the `Graph` constructor takes a Polars edge list with `edges_df=`.
  [Learn more](building-graphs.qmd#building-a-graph-from-an-edge-list).

Edge table
: The Polars DataFrame with one row per edge returned by `get_edge_df()`. Its first columns are
  `id`, `source`, `target`, and `rel`, followed by `weight` when any edge has one and then the other
  edge **attributes**. The `source` and `target` columns hold **node IDs**. The table is a copy, so
  changing it never changes the graph. `get_edge_df_ws()` gives the rows of the selected edges only.
  See also **node table**. [Learn more](node-and-edge-data.qmd#the-node-and-edge-tables).

Efficiency
: The mean of the reciprocal **distances** between all pairs of nodes. Unlike the **mean distance**,
  it stays finite when the graph is disconnected, since unreachable pairs contribute 0. *Local
  efficiency* measures the efficiency of each node's neighborhood without the node itself. Available
  via `global_efficiency()` and `local_efficiency()`. [Learn more](structure.qmd#distances).

Ego network
: The **subgraph** made up of one node (the *ego*), its neighbors (the *alters*), and the edges
  among them, possibly extended to neighbors of neighbors. Ego networks are the standard unit of
  personal network studies. Available via `ego_graph()`, whose `radius=` sets how many steps out to
  go. [Learn more](transforming.qmd#ego-networks).

Eigenvector centrality
: A **centrality** in which a node is important when it is linked to other important nodes. The
  scores are the entries of the leading eigenvector of the **adjacency matrix**. Available via
  `eigen_centrality()`. See also **PageRank**, **Katz centrality**, and **hubs and authorities**.
  [Learn more](centrality.qmd#spectral-centrality).

Enrichment
: A statistical test of whether a group of nodes, such as a **community** or a **disease module**,
  contains more nodes of some category than chance would produce, usually with a hypergeometric
  test. It is how modules of genes are linked to known biological functions. Available via
  `subgraph_enrichment()` and `module_annotation_enrichment()`, which tests every community at once
  with a correction for multiple testing. [Learn
  more](network-biology.qmd#interpreting-modules-with-annotations).

Epidemic threshold
: The transmission rate below which an infection dies out and above which it can reach a sizable
  share of a network. For the **SIR model** on a network of random structure, the threshold of the
  transmissibility is $T_c = \langle k \rangle / (\langle k^2 \rangle - \langle k \rangle)$, where
  $\langle k \rangle$ and $\langle k^2 \rangle$ are the mean **degree** and mean squared degree, so
  networks with **hubs** have a much lower threshold. For SIS dynamics, the threshold is roughly the
  reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of the **adjacency matrix**. See also **percolation**. [Learn
  more](spreading.qmd#the-epidemic-threshold).

Erdős–Rényi model
: See **random graph**.

Eulerian path
: A **trail** that uses every edge exactly once; an *Eulerian circuit* also ends where it starts. A
  connected graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when every node has even **degree**, as Euler
  showed for the bridges of Königsberg. Available via `has_eulerian_path()`, `eulerian_path()`,
  `is_eulerian()`, `eulerian_circuit()`, and `eulerize()`, which adds the fewest edges needed to
  make a graph Eulerian. [Learn more](paths.qmd#eulerian-paths-and-circuits).

Fiedler vector
: The eigenvector of the **Laplacian matrix** that belongs to the **algebraic connectivity**. Its
  entries place the nodes along a line so that linked nodes are close, and splitting the nodes by
  its sign gives a good cut of the graph in two. Available via `fiedler_vector()`,
  `spectral_ordering()`, and `spectral_bisection()`. [Learn
  more](spectral.qmd#ordering-nodes-with-the-fiedler-vector).

Flow
: An assignment of amounts to the edges of a network with capacities, such as pipes or roads, that
  respects each edge's capacity and conserves the amount at every node except a source and a sink.
  The *maximum flow* is the most that can be sent from the source to the sink, and equals the
  capacity of the **minimum cut** between them. A *minimum-cost flow* meets given demands at the
  lowest cost. Available via `maximum_flow()`, `maximum_flow_value()`, and `minimum_cost_flow()`.
  [Learn more](connectivity.qmd#flows).

Force-directed layout
: A **layout** that treats the edges as springs and the nodes as mutually repelling particles, and
  lets the system settle. Linked nodes end up close and groups of densely linked nodes form visible
  clusters. Available via `layout_spring()` (Fruchterman–Reingold), `layout_kamada_kawai()`, and
  `layout_forceatlas2()`. [Learn more](layouts.qmd#force-directed-layouts).

Forest
: An undirected graph without **cycles**, so that each of its **components** is a **tree**.
  Available via `is_forest()`. [Learn more](dags.qmd#trees).

Generator
: A method that adds a graph of a given structure or a random graph from a given model, such as a
  grid, a tree, a **small world**, or a **stochastic block model**. EdgeCase's generators are
  methods whose names start with `add_`, such as `add_grid_2d()`, `add_gnp_graph()`, and
  `add_pa_graph()`, and they add to the graph they are called on, so several can be combined in one
  graph. The random generators take `seed=` for reproducible results. [Learn
  more](generators.qmd).

Giant component
: A **component** that holds a sizable share of all the nodes, as opposed to the many small
  components that hold only a handful each. Its appearance as edges are added, or its collapse as
  nodes and edges are removed, is a phase transition studied by **percolation** theory. Available
  via `largest_component_size()`. See also **Molloy–Reed criterion**. [Learn
  more](spreading.qmd#outbreaks-as-percolation).

Girth
: The length of the shortest **cycle** in a graph. A graph without cycles has infinite girth.
  Available via `girth()`. [Learn more](clustering-and-motifs.qmd#cycles).

Girvan–Newman method
: A **community detection** method that repeatedly removes the edge of highest edge **betweenness
  centrality**, the edges most likely to lie between communities, until the network falls apart into
  groups. It is accurate but slow on large networks. Available via `cmty_girvan_newman()` and
  `cmty_edge_btwns()`. [Learn more](communities.qmd#detection-algorithms).

Graph
: A set of **nodes** together with a set of **edges** that link pairs of them. Also called a
  *network*, especially when it describes a real-world system. In EdgeCase, a graph is an `ec.Graph`
  object, created empty with `ec.Graph()` and filled with nodes and edges, or built from data, a
  **generator**, or a **dataset**. It can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted, and may
  contain **parallel edges** and **self-loops**. Printing a graph shows a summary of its size and of
  the results stored on it, and `describe()` prints a fuller overview. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd).

Graph edit distance
: The smallest number of edits, such as adding or deleting nodes and edges, that turns one graph
  into another. It measures how different two graphs are, but is expensive to compute exactly.
  Available via `graph_edit_distance()` and `optimize_graph_edit_distance()`. [Learn
  more](similarity.qmd#measuring-differences).

Graph product
: A way of combining two graphs into a larger one whose nodes are the pairs of their nodes. The
  *Cartesian product* of two paths is a grid, and of two cycles a torus; the tensor, strong, and
  lexicographic products link the pairs by other rules. Available via `cartesian_product()`,
  `tensor_product()`, `strong_product()`, and `lexicographic_product()`. [Learn
  more](transforming.qmd#products).

Graph widget
: An interactive view of a graph, drawn on an HTML canvas in a notebook, that can be dragged,
  panned, and zoomed, with colors and sizes mapped from the data and tooltips on hover. Available
  via `graph_widget()`, which returns a `GraphWidget`. See also **step player**. [Learn
  more](interactive.qmd#the-graph-widget).

Great Tables
: A Python package, installed together with EdgeCase, that turns a data frame into a formatted,
  publication-ready table. It is the natural way to present the **node table**, the **edge table**,
  and summaries computed from them. [Learn more](tables.qmd#presenting-tables-with-great-tables).

Harmonic centrality
: A **centrality** that sums the reciprocal **distances** from a node to all others. It is a variant
  of **closeness centrality** that handles disconnected graphs, since an unreachable node adds
  nothing to the sum. Available via `harmonic_centrality()`. [Learn
  more](centrality.qmd#closeness-and-harmonic-centrality).

Heat diffusion
: A **network propagation** method that places heat on seed nodes and lets it flow along the edges
  for a time $t$, following the heat equation on the **Laplacian matrix**. Short times keep the heat
  near the seeds, and longer times spread it further. Available via `heat_diffusion()`. See also
  **random walk with restart**. [Learn more](network-biology.qmd#heat-diffusion).

Homophily
: The tendency of nodes to link to nodes that share their attributes, such as people of the same age
  or the same opinions. It is measured by the **assortativity** of a categorical attribute or by a
  **mixing matrix**. [Learn more](structure.qmd#mixing-patterns).

Hub
: A node of much higher **degree** than most, a common feature of networks with heavy-tailed
  **degree distributions**. Hubs hold networks together, which makes them resilient to random
  failures and fragile to targeted attacks (see **robustness**), and they speed up **spreading**.
  See also **hubs and authorities**. [Learn more](spreading.qmd#two-networks).

Hubs and authorities
: A pair of scores for the nodes of a directed graph, computed by the HITS algorithm. A good
  *authority* is pointed to by good hubs, and a good *hub* points to good authorities, as with the
  reference pages and the review pages of the web. Available via `hub_centrality()` and
  `authority_centrality()`. [Learn more](centrality.qmd#hubs-and-authorities).

Immunization
: Removing nodes from a network, as by vaccination, to stop an epidemic from spreading. *Random*
  immunization needs a large share of the nodes on a network with **hubs**, *targeted* immunization
  of the hubs needs far fewer, and *acquaintance* immunization, which immunizes a random neighbor of
  each randomly chosen node, finds the hubs without knowing the network. See also **epidemic
  threshold**. [Learn more](spreading.qmd#immunization).

Incidence matrix
: A matrix with one row per node and one column per edge, whose entries mark which nodes each edge
  joins. Available via `incidence_matrix()`. See also **adjacency matrix**. [Learn
  more](spectral.qmd#graphs-as-matrices).

Independent cascade
: A model of spreading in which each newly activated node gets a single chance to activate each of
  its inactive neighbors, succeeding with a fixed probability. It is equivalent to edge
  **percolation**: the final set of activated nodes is the **component** of the seeds in a graph
  that keeps each edge with that probability. It underlies **influence maximization**. See also
  **SIR model**. [Learn more](spreading.qmd#influential-spreaders).

Independent set
: A set of nodes of which no two are linked. A *maximal* independent set can't be extended, and a
  *maximum* one is a largest; the complement of an independent set is a **vertex cover**. Available
  via `maximal_independent_set()`, `maximum_independent_set()`, and `is_independent_set()`. [Learn
  more](coloring-matching.qmd#vertex-covers-and-independent-sets).

Induced subgraph
: See **subgraph**.

Influence maximization
: Choosing a set of $k$ seed nodes that, when activated, spread an influence to as many nodes as
  possible under a model such as the **independent cascade**. The greedy algorithm, which adds the
  node that raises the expected spread the most at each step, is the standard method. Available via
  `influence_maximization()`. See also **VoteRank**. [Learn
  more](spreading.qmd#influential-spreaders).

Isolate
: A node without any edges, of **degree** 0. Available via `isolates()`. [Learn
  more](connectivity.qmd#connected-components).

Isomorphism
: A one-to-one mapping between the nodes of two graphs that preserves every edge. Two graphs are
  *isomorphic* when such a mapping exists, which means that they have the same structure under
  different names. *Subgraph isomorphism* finds one graph as a part of another. Available via
  `is_isomorphic()`, `find_isomorphism()`, `is_subgraph_isomorphic()`, `subgraph_isomorphisms()`,
  and `weisfeiler_lehman_graph_hash()` for a quick fingerprint. See also **automorphism**. [Learn
  more](similarity.qmd#isomorphism).

Jaccard similarity
: The **similarity** of two nodes measured as the number of their **common neighbors** divided by
  the number of nodes linked to either of them. It runs from 0 (no shared neighbors) to 1 (identical
  neighborhoods). Available via `jaccard_similarity()` and `jaccard_coefficient()`. See also
  **structural equivalence**. [Learn more](similarity.qmd#neighborhood-similarity).

k-core
: The largest **subgraph** in which every node has **degree** at least $k$, found by repeatedly
  removing the nodes of smaller degree. The cores are nested, and the innermost ones mark the dense
  center of a network. Available via `k_core()`, with `k_shell()`, `k_crust()`, and `k_corona()` for
  related parts. See also **coreness** and **k-truss**. [Learn
  more](structure.qmd#cores-and-dense-regions).

k-truss
: The largest **subgraph** in which every edge lies in at least $k - 2$ **triangles**. It is a
  stricter notion of a cohesive group than the **k-core**, and sits between the k-core and the
  **clique**. Available via `k_truss()`. [Learn more](structure.qmd#cores-and-dense-regions).

Katz centrality
: A **centrality** that counts all the **walks** that end at a node, with longer walks counting less
  by a factor $\alpha$ per step. Unlike **eigenvector centrality**, it gives every node some score,
  which suits directed graphs. Available via `katz_centrality()`, with the related
  `alpha_centrality()`. [Learn more](centrality.qmd#spectral-centrality).

Label
: The optional, human-readable string name of a node, such as `"Ada"` or `"BRCA1"`. Labels are
  unique within a graph and always strings, so a node added as `add_node(7)` is labelled `"7"`.
  Wherever a method takes a node, a `str` is read as a label and an `int` as a **node ID**. Labels
  are changed with `relabel_nodes()`, and converted to and from IDs with `get_id_from_label()` and
  `get_label_from_id()`. A *label* in Cypher is a different thing: Cypher reads a node's **type** as
  its label. [Learn more](graph-model.qmd#labels).

Label propagation
: A fast **community detection** method in which every node repeatedly adopts the community most
  common among its neighbors, until the communities stop changing. Its results vary from run to run.
  Available via `cmty_label_propagation()`, `cmty_fast_label_propagation()`, and
  `cmty_semisync_label_propagation()`. [Learn more](communities.qmd#detection-algorithms).

Laplacian matrix
: The matrix $L = D - A$, where $D$ holds the node **degrees** on its diagonal and $A$ is the
  **adjacency matrix**. Its eigenvalues describe how well connected a graph is, how it can be cut,
  and how processes such as diffusion spread on it; the number of zero eigenvalues is the number of
  **components**. Available via `laplacian_matrix()`, `normalized_laplacian_matrix()`, and
  `laplacian_spectrum()`. See also **algebraic connectivity** and **Fiedler vector**. [Learn
  more](spectral.qmd#the-laplacian-and-its-relatives).

Layer
: See **multiplex network**.

Layout
: The positions of the nodes in a drawing. A layout method computes the positions and stores them in
  the `pos` node attribute, which `plot(layout="pos")` reuses, so that several drawings can share
  the same positions. Available via the `layout_*()` methods, such as `layout_spring()`,
  `layout_circular()`, `layout_bipartite()`, and `layout_spectral()`. See also **force-directed
  layout**. [Learn more](layouts.qmd).

Leiden method
: A **community detection** method that refines the **Louvain method** so that every community it
  finds is internally connected. It optimizes **modularity** or the constant Potts model. Available
  via `cmty_leiden()`, with `cmty_leiden_levels()` for the hierarchy of levels. [Learn
  more](communities.qmd#detection-algorithms).

Line graph
: The graph whose nodes are the edges of another graph, with two of them linked when the edges share
  an endpoint. It turns questions about edges into questions about nodes. Available via
  `line_graph()`. [Learn more](transforming.qmd#derived-graphs).

Link prediction
: Estimating which missing edges are likely to exist or to form, from the structure of the edges
  that are known. Most predictors score pairs of nodes by their **similarity**, such as their
  **common neighbors**, **Jaccard similarity**, or **Adamic–Adar index**. Available via
  `adamic_adar_index()`, `resource_allocation_index()`, `jaccard_coefficient()`, and
  `preferential_attachment()`, among others. [Learn more](similarity.qmd#link-prediction).

Local bridge
: See **bridge**.

Louvain method
: A fast **community detection** method that maximizes **modularity** in passes: it moves single
  nodes between communities while the modularity improves, then merges each community into a single
  node and repeats on the smaller network. Its **resolution** sets the size of the communities.
  Available via `cmty_louvain()`, with `cmty_louvain_levels()` for the hierarchy of levels. See also
  **Leiden method**. [Learn more](communities.qmd#detection-algorithms).

Lowest common ancestor
: For two nodes of a **DAG** or a rooted **tree**, the common **ancestor** that is closest to them,
  such as the most recent common ancestor of two species. Available via `lowest_common_ancestor()`
  and `all_pairs_lowest_common_ancestor()`. [Learn more](dags.qmd#lowest-common-ancestors).

Matching
: A set of edges of which no two share a node, so that each node is paired with at most one other. A
  *maximum* matching pairs as many nodes as possible, a *perfect* matching pairs them all, and a
  maximum-weight matching maximizes the total **weight** of the pairs. In a **bipartite graph**,
  matching solves assignment problems, such as workers to jobs. Available via
  `maximum_weight_matching()`, `maximal_matching()`, `bipartite_maximum_matching()`, and
  `bipartite_minimum_weight_full_matching()`. [Learn more](coloring-matching.qmd#matching).

Maximum cut
: A division of the nodes into two groups that maximizes the number, or the total weight, of the
  edges between them. Available via `maximum_cut()`. See also **minimum cut**. [Learn
  more](coloring-matching.qmd#maximum-cut).

Mean distance
: The mean **distance** over all pairs of nodes that are connected, also called the *average path
  length*. It grows only slowly with the size of a network (see **small world**). Available via
  `mean_distance()`. See also **diameter** and **efficiency**. [Learn
  more](structure.qmd#distances).

Minimum cut
: The smallest set of edges (or nodes) whose removal separates two given nodes, or disconnects the
  graph; in a **weighted graph**, the set of smallest total weight. Its size is the **connectivity**
  between the nodes and equals the maximum **flow** between them. Available via `minimum_cut()`,
  `minimum_edge_cut()`, `minimum_node_cut()`, `minimum_cut_value()`, and `stoer_wagner()` for the
  global minimum cut of a weighted graph. [Learn more](connectivity.qmd#flows).

Mixing matrix
: A table that counts the share of edges between each pair of attribute values or degrees, such as
  the share of friendships between members of two factions. Its pattern shows **homophily** and
  **assortativity** in detail. Available via `attribute_mixing_matrix()` and
  `degree_mixing_matrix()`. [Learn more](structure.qmd#mixing-patterns).

Modularity
: A score for a **partition** of the nodes into **communities**: the share of edges that fall within
  communities minus the share expected if the edges were placed at random with the same **degrees**,

  $$
  Q = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{ij} \left( A_{ij} - \gamma \frac{k_i k_j}{2m} \right) \delta(c_i, c_j),
  $$

  where $m$ is the number of edges, $k_i$ the degree of node $i$, $c_i$ its community, and $\gamma$
  the **resolution**. Values above about 0.3 suggest clear community structure. Most community
  detection methods try to maximize it. Available via `modularity()`, with `partition_quality()` for
  two other scores. [Learn more](communities.qmd#measuring-the-quality-of-a-partition).

Molloy–Reed criterion
: The condition under which a network of random structure with a given **degree distribution** has a
  **giant component**: $\langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle > 2$. Applied to random failures, it
  predicts the share of nodes whose removal breaks the giant component, $1 - 1 / (\kappa - 1)$ with
  $\kappa = \langle k^2 \rangle / \langle k \rangle$, which approaches 1 for networks with **hubs**.
  See also **robustness** and **percolation**. [Learn
  more](spreading.qmd#the-threshold-of-random-failure).

Motif
: A small pattern of connections, such as a triangle or a feed-forward loop, that occurs in a
  network much more often than in comparable **random graphs**. Motifs are thought to be building
  blocks with particular functions, especially in biological networks. Available via
  `motif_census()`, which counts every pattern of a given size, and `motif_significance()`, which
  compares the counts with a **null model**. See also **triad**. [Learn
  more](clustering-and-motifs.qmd#motifs).

Multigraph
: A graph that may have several edges between the same pair of nodes. Any EdgeCase graph can hold
  **parallel edges**, so there is no separate multigraph class. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#parallel-edges-and-self-loops).

Multiplex network
: A network in which the same nodes are linked by several kinds of tie, such as working together,
  friendship, and advice among colleagues. Each kind of tie forms a *layer*. In EdgeCase, a
  multiplex network can be one graph whose edge **rel** names each edge's layer, or a
  `MultiplexGraph` that holds the layers as separate graphs on the same nodes, with
  `multiplex_pagerank()` and `multiplex_community_detection()` analyzing the layers together. See
  also **multiplexity**. [Learn more](multiplex.qmd).

Multiplexity
: The number of **layers** in which a pair of nodes is linked. Pairs with several kinds of tie are
  usually closer and more stable than pairs with one. [Learn
  more](multiplex.qmd#describing-the-layers-together).

Neighbor
: A node linked to a given node by an edge. In a **directed graph**, the nodes that an edge points
  to are the node's *successors*, and those that point to it are its *predecessors*. The set of a
  node's neighbors is its *neighborhood*. Available via `get_neighbors()`, `get_successors()`, and
  `get_predecessors()`, with `select_nodes_in_neighborhood()` selecting a neighborhood. [Learn
  more](traversals.qmd#neighbors).

Network
: See **graph**.

Network propagation
: A family of methods that spread scores from some nodes over a network, so that nodes near
  high-scoring nodes score highly too. It is used to prioritize candidate disease genes from known
  ones and to smooth noisy measurements, such as association scores, using the network as a guide.
  Available via `random_walk_with_restart()`, `heat_diffusion()`, `personalized_pagerank()`, and
  `network_smooth()`. [Learn more](network-biology.qmd#prioritizing-candidate-genes).

Network proximity
: The closeness of two sets of nodes in a network, such as the targets of a drug and the genes of a
  disease, measured from the **distances** between them. A drug whose targets are closer to a
  disease's genes than chance would place them is a candidate for treating it. Available via
  `network_proximity()`. [Learn more](network-biology.qmd#network-proximity-of-drugs).

Node
: One of the objects that a graph links, such as a person, a web page, or a protein. Also called a
  *vertex*, or an *actor* in social networks. Every node in EdgeCase has a **node ID**, an optional
  **label**, an optional **type**, and any number of **attributes**. Nodes are added with
  `add_node()` and `add_nodes()`, and fetched as `Node` objects with `get_node()`. Asking for a node
  that doesn't exist raises a `NodeNotFoundError`. [Learn more](graph-model.qmd#nodes).

Node ID
: The positive integer that EdgeCase assigns to each node, starting from 1 in the order the nodes
  are added. IDs are never reused, even after a node is deleted, so an ID always refers to the same
  node. Methods that return nodes, such as `get_neighbors()` and `shortest_path()`, return IDs, and
  methods with `return_dict=True` key their results by ID. Wherever a method takes a node, an `int`
  is read as an ID and a `str` as a **label**. See also **edge ID**. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#ids).

Node table
: The Polars DataFrame with one row per node returned by `get_node_df()`. Its first columns are
  `id`, `label`, and `type`, followed by the node **attributes** in alphabetical order and a
  `degree` column computed on the spot. The table is a copy, so changing it never changes the graph;
  results computed from it are written back with `set_node_attrs()`. `get_node_df_ws()` gives the
  rows of the selected nodes only. See also **edge table**. [Learn
  more](node-and-edge-data.qmd#the-node-and-edge-tables).

Normalized mutual information (NMI)
: A measure of the agreement between two **partitions** of the same nodes, such as detected
  communities and known groups. It is 1 for identical partitions and close to 0 for unrelated ones.
  [Learn more](communities.qmd#comparing-with-known-groups).

Null model
: A random graph that keeps some properties of a real network, such as its number of edges or its
  **degrees**, and randomizes the rest. Comparing the network with its null model shows which of its
  features are surprising and which follow from the properties kept. Available via
  `random_reference()`, `lattice_reference()`, `configuration_model()`, and
  `degree_preserving_rewire()`. See also **rewiring**. [Learn
  more](generators.qmd#null-models-from-an-existing-graph).

PageRank
: A **centrality** that scores a node by the share of time a random surfer spends at it, where the
  surfer follows a random outgoing edge with probability $d$ (the *damping factor*, 0.85 by default)
  and jumps to a random node otherwise. Developed to rank web pages, it is a variant of
  **eigenvector centrality** that works on directed graphs. Available via `pagerank()`. See also
  **personalized PageRank**. [Learn more](centrality.qmd#pagerank).

Parallel edges
: Two or more edges that join the same pair of nodes (in the same direction, in a directed graph).
  They represent repeated interactions or ties of different kinds, such as the layers of a
  **multiplex network**. Every EdgeCase graph allows them, and **edge IDs** tell them apart.
  Available via `count_multi_edges()` and `which_multiple()`, with `remove_duplicate_edges()` and
  `simplify()` to remove them. See also **simple graph**. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#parallel-edges-and-self-loops).

Partition
: A division of the nodes into groups, with each node in exactly one group, such as the result of
  **community detection**. EdgeCase stores a partition as a node attribute holding each node's group
  number, and the methods that score partitions, such as `modularity()`, take the name of that
  attribute, a dictionary of groups keyed by node, or a list of the groups. See also **quotient
  graph**. [Learn more](communities.qmd#working-with-the-results).

Path
: A sequence of nodes in which each is linked to the next. In a *simple path*, no node appears
  twice. More generally, a **walk** may repeat nodes and edges, and a **trail** may repeat nodes but
  not edges. Available via `has_path()`, `shortest_path()`, `all_simple_paths()`, and
  `is_simple_path()`. See also **shortest path** and **cycle**. [Learn more](paths.qmd).

Percolation
: The study of what remains connected when a random share of a network's edges (*bond* percolation)
  or nodes (*site* percolation) is removed. As the share removed grows, the **giant component**
  shrinks and then disappears at a *percolation threshold*. Percolation describes both the failure
  of networks and the spread of epidemics, since an outbreak spreads over the edges that transmit.
  Available via `edge_percolation()`, `node_percolation()`, and `percolation_threshold_analysis()`.
  See also **robustness**, **epidemic threshold**, and **Molloy–Reed criterion**. [Learn
  more](spreading.qmd#outbreaks-as-percolation).

Personalized PageRank
: A version of **PageRank** in which the random surfer jumps back to a chosen set of nodes rather
  than to any node, so that the scores measure closeness to those nodes. It is the same idea as a
  **random walk with restart**. Available via `personalized_pagerank()`. [Learn
  more](centrality.qmd#pagerank).

Planar graph
: A graph that can be drawn in the plane without any edges crossing, such as a road network without
  bridges or tunnels. Available via `is_planar()`, `check_planarity()`, and `layout_planar()`.
  [Learn more](coloring-matching.qmd#planar-graphs).

Polars
: The DataFrame library that EdgeCase uses for its tables. The **node table** and the **edge table**
  are Polars DataFrames, graphs can be built from Polars tables of nodes and edges, and Cypher
  queries return their matches as Polars DataFrames. [Learn more](node-and-edge-data.qmd).

Predecessor
: See **neighbor**.

Preferential attachment
: A model of network growth in which each new node links to existing nodes with probabilities
  proportional to their **degrees**, so that the well-connected get better connected. Its standard
  form, the Barabási–Albert model, produces a **scale-free network** with **hubs**. Available via
  `add_pa_graph()`, with variants such as `add_dual_barabasi_albert_graph()` and
  `add_powerlaw_cluster_graph()`. As a **link prediction** score, *preferential attachment* is the
  product of the two degrees, available via `preferential_attachment()`. [Learn
  more](generators.qmd#the-classic-models).

Prize-collecting Steiner tree
: See **Steiner tree**.

Projection
: A one-mode network derived from a **bipartite graph** by linking two nodes of one side when they
  share a neighbor on the other: two people who attended the same event, or two diseases linked to
  the same gene. The edges are usually weighted by the number of shared neighbors. Available via
  `bipartite_projection()`. [Learn more](transforming.qmd#derived-graphs).

Quotient graph
: The graph formed by collapsing each group of a **partition** into a single node, with an edge
  between two groups when any of their members are linked. It gives a zoomed-out view of a network,
  such as a network of communities. Available via `quotient_graph()`, with `contract_nodes()` for
  merging a single group. [Learn more](communities.qmd#a-network-of-communities).

Radius
: The smallest **eccentricity** of any node, the distance from the **center** to the node farthest
  from it. Available via `radius()`. See also **diameter**. [Learn
  more](structure.qmd#distances).

Random graph
: A graph generated by a random process. In the Erdős–Rényi model, $G(n, p)$ links each pair of $n$
  nodes independently with probability $p$, and $G(n, m)$ places $m$ edges among the pairs at
  random. Such graphs have small distances but little clustering and no **hubs**, and serve as the
  baseline against which real networks are compared. Available via `add_gnp_graph()` and
  `add_gnm_graph()`. See also **configuration model**, **null model**, and **stochastic block
  model**. [Learn more](generators.qmd#random-graphs).

Random walk
: A **walk** that moves from each node to a randomly chosen neighbor. Random walks underlie
  **PageRank**, diffusion, the **resistance distance**, and community detection methods such as
  Walktrap, which finds groups in which walks tend to stay. Available via `random_walk()` and
  `random_edge_walk()`. [Learn more](paths.qmd#walks).

Random walk with restart (RWR)
: A **random walk** that returns to a set of seed nodes with a fixed probability at every step. The
  share of time it spends at each node measures the node's closeness to the seeds, taking all paths
  into account, and is used to prioritize candidate disease genes. Available via
  `random_walk_with_restart()`, whose `restart_prob=` is 0.15 by default. See also **network
  propagation** and **personalized PageRank**. [Learn
  more](network-biology.qmd#random-walk-with-restart).

Reachability
: Whether a path leads from one node to another. In a **directed graph**, reachability need not be
  symmetric. Available via `has_path()`, `descendants()`, and `reachability_index()`, which answers
  many reachability queries quickly. See also **transitive closure**. [Learn
  more](dags.qmd#reachability-queries).

Reciprocity
: The share of the edges of a **directed graph** whose reverse edge is also present, such as
  friendship nominations that are returned. Available via `reciprocity()`, with `which_mutual()`
  and `count_mutual_node_pairs()`. [Learn more](structure.qmd#reciprocity).

Regular graph
: A graph in which every node has the same **degree**, $k$ for a *k-regular* graph. Available via
  `is_regular()`, `is_k_regular()`, and `add_random_regular_graph()`. [Learn
  more](structure.qmd#properties).

rel
: The relationship type of an edge, such as `"friend"` or `"cites"`, stored in the `rel` column of
  the **edge table**. Like the node **type**, it has a special role: **Cypher** queries read it as
  the relationship type (as in `-[:friend]->`), many methods can filter on it, and it can record the
  layer of each edge in a **multiplex network**. It is set with the `rel=` argument of `add_edge()`,
  `add_edges()`, and the **generators**. [Learn
  more](node-and-edge-data.qmd#types-and-relationship-types).

Resistance distance
: The **distance** between two nodes measured as the electrical resistance between them when every
  edge is a one-ohm resistor. Unlike the **shortest path** distance, it falls when there are many
  routes between the nodes, and it is related to **random walks**. Available via
  `resistance_distance()`, `resistance_distance_matrix()`, and `kirchhoff_index()`, the sum
  over all pairs. [Learn more](paths.qmd#resistance-distance).

Resolution
: A parameter of **modularity** and of the community detection methods that maximize it, written
  $\gamma$, that sets the scale of the communities found. Values above 1 give more and smaller
  communities, and values below 1 fewer and larger ones. Available as the `resolution=` argument of
  `cmty_louvain()`, `cmty_leiden()`, and `modularity()`. [Learn
  more](communities.qmd#resolution).

Resource allocation index
: A **link prediction** score for a pair of nodes that sums $1 / k$ over their **common neighbors**,
  where $k$ is the neighbor's **degree**, imagining each neighbor dividing a resource among its
  ties. It is similar to the **Adamic–Adar index** but penalizes hubs more. Available via
  `resource_allocation_index()`. [Learn more](similarity.qmd#link-prediction).

return_dict
: The argument, accepted by the methods that compute a value for every node, that returns the
  results as a dictionary keyed by **node ID** instead of storing them on the graph. See **stored
  results**. [Learn more](get-started.qmd#three-ideas-that-run-through-the-library).

Rewiring
: Randomly swapping the endpoints of pairs of edges, so that the edges change but every node keeps
  its **degree**. Repeated many times, it turns a network into a sample from its degree-preserving
  **null model**. Available via `degree_preserving_rewire()` and `random_reference()`. See also
  **configuration model**. [Learn more](generators.qmd#null-models-from-an-existing-graph).

Rich club
: The tendency of the high-degree nodes of a network to be densely linked to each other, as when the
  most prominent scientists all collaborate. The *rich-club coefficient* is the **density** among
  the nodes above each degree, best compared with that of a **null model**. Available via
  `rich_club_coefficient()`. [Learn more](structure.qmd#rich-clubs).

Robustness
: How well a network stays connected as nodes or edges fail or are removed, usually measured by the
  size of the **giant component** as more and more are removed. Networks with **hubs** are robust to
  random failures but fragile to attacks on the hubs. The *robustness index* $R$ averages the share
  of nodes in the giant component over all stages of the removal. Available via
  `network_robustness()`, which removes nodes in order of **degree**, betweenness, or at random, and
  `node_percolation()`. See also **percolation** and **Molloy–Reed criterion**. [Learn
  more](spreading.qmd#robustness).

Scale-free network
: A network whose **degree distribution** follows a power law, $p(k) \propto k^{-\gamma}$, at least
  in its tail, so that it has **hubs** of every size and no typical degree. Such networks arise from
  **preferential attachment**. How common exact power laws are in real networks is debated, but
  heavy-tailed degree distributions are widespread. Available via `add_pa_graph()` and
  `add_scale_free_graph()`. [Learn more](generators.qmd#the-classic-models).

Selection
: A set of nodes, or a set of edges, that a graph holds as part of its state, so that a later call
  can act on it. The `select_*()` methods build a selection, by attribute, degree, centrality,
  pattern, or ID; the `trav_*()` methods move it along the edges; and the methods whose names end in
  `_ws` ("with selection") act on it, such as `set_node_attrs_ws()` or `delete_nodes_ws()`. A graph
  selects either nodes or edges, never both, and a selection persists until it is changed or cleared
  with `clear_selection()`. See also **traversal**. [Learn more](selections.qmd).

Self-loop
: An edge that joins a node to itself. Self-loops represent, for example, a gene that regulates
  itself. EdgeCase allows them in any graph. Available via `count_loops()`, `which_loops()`, and
  `remove_selfloops()`. See also **simple graph**. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#parallel-edges-and-self-loops).

Shortest path
: A **path** between two nodes with the fewest edges, or in a **weighted graph** the smallest total
  **weight**. Its length is the **distance** between the nodes, and there may be several shortest
  paths of the same length. Available via `shortest_path()`, `shortest_path_length()`,
  `all_shortest_paths()`, and `k_shortest_paths()` for the next-best alternatives. See also
  **Dijkstra's algorithm** and **A\* search**. [Learn
  more](paths.qmd#the-shortest-path-between-two-nodes).

Similarity
: A measure of how alike two nodes are, based on their positions in the network rather than their
  attributes. Neighborhood measures, such as **Jaccard similarity** and cosine similarity, compare
  the nodes' **neighbors**, and path-based measures, such as **SimRank**, take more distant
  structure into account. Available via `jaccard_similarity()`, `cosine_similarity()`,
  `dice_similarity()`, `pairwise_similarity()`, and `simrank_similarity()`. See also **link
  prediction** and **structural equivalence**. [Learn more](similarity.qmd).

Simple graph
: A graph without **parallel edges** or **self-loops**. Many algorithms and file formats assume a
  simple graph. Available via `is_simple()` and `simplify()`, which removes both. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#parallel-edges-and-self-loops).

SimRank
: A **similarity** in which two nodes are similar when their **neighbors** are similar, computed
  recursively, with every node maximally similar to itself. Available via `simrank_similarity()`.
  [Learn more](similarity.qmd#similarity-from-paths).

SIR model
: A model of an epidemic in which every node is *susceptible*, *infected*, or *recovered*. Each
  infected node infects each susceptible neighbor with some probability, and then recovers and
  cannot be infected again. Its final outbreak size relates to **percolation**, and its behavior
  depends on whether the transmissibility is above the **epidemic threshold**. In the related SIS
  model, recovered nodes become susceptible again. See also **independent cascade** and
  **immunization**. [Learn more](spreading.qmd#simulating-an-epidemic).

Site percolation
: See **percolation**.

Small world
: A network in which most nodes can be reached from any other in a few steps, even though the
  network is large and most nodes have few ties, as in the "six degrees of separation" of social
  networks. The Watts–Strogatz model shows how a few random shortcuts give a clustered lattice small
  distances. Small-world networks combine a high **clustering coefficient** with a short **mean
  distance**. Available via `add_smallworld_graph()`, `small_world_sigma()`, and
  `small_world_omega()`. [Learn more](structure.qmd#small-worlds).

Soft thresholding
: The step of **co-expression network** construction in WGCNA that raises the absolute correlations
  between genes to a power $\beta$, so that weak correlations fade while strong ones are kept. The
  power is chosen as the smallest one that makes the network approximately scale-free (see
  **scale-free network**). Available via `soft_threshold_power()`. [Learn
  more](network-biology.qmd#choosing-the-power).

Source
: The node at which an edge starts; the node at which it ends is its *target*. In a **directed
  graph**, the edge points from the source to the target. In an **undirected graph**, the two are
  interchangeable, but EdgeCase still records them in the order the endpoints were given. The
  `source` and `target` columns of the **edge table** hold **node IDs**. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#edges).

Spanning tree
: A **tree** that includes every node of a connected graph and uses some of its edges. A *minimum
  spanning tree* has the smallest total **weight**, the cheapest way to connect everything, as with
  a network of cables. Available via `minimum_spanning_tree()`, `maximum_spanning_tree()`,
  `number_of_spanning_trees()`, and `random_spanning_tree()`. See also **arborescence** and
  **Steiner tree**. [Learn more](connectivity.qmd#spanning-trees).

Sparse graph
: See **density**.

Spectrum
: The eigenvalues of a matrix of a graph, usually the **adjacency matrix** or the **Laplacian
  matrix**. The spectrum reflects many structural properties: the number of **components**, whether
  it is a **bipartite graph**, how well the graph can be cut, and the number of communities.
  Available via `adjacency_spectrum()`, `laplacian_spectrum()`, `modularity_spectrum()`, and
  `bethe_hessian_spectrum()`. [Learn more](spectral.qmd).

Spreading
: Any process by which something passes along the edges of a network: an infection, a rumor, a
  behavior, or a failure. Its reach depends on the structure of the network, especially its
  **hubs**. See also **SIR model**, **independent cascade**, **epidemic threshold**, and **influence
  maximization**. [Learn more](spreading.qmd).

Steiner tree
: The smallest **tree** that connects a given set of *terminal* nodes, possibly through other nodes.
  The *prize-collecting* variant gives each node a prize and each edge a cost, and finds the tree
  that best trades off the prizes collected against the costs paid; it is used to extract **disease
  modules** from gene scores. Available via `steiner_tree()`, `prize_collecting_steiner_tree()`, and
  `directed_steiner_tree()`. See also **spanning tree**. [Learn more](paths.qmd#steiner-trees).

Step
: A single entry of the **step log**, recorded for each call that builds, changes, analyzes, or
  traverses a graph. A step holds the method that was called, a snippet of code that shows the call,
  a narration, the nodes and edges it affected, and its *kind*, such as `"build_nodes"`, `"metric"`,
  or `"select"`. A traversal is recorded as one step with a *sub-step* for every node it visited.
  [Learn more](step-log.qmd#steps-in-detail).

Step log
: The record of everything that has been done to a graph, kept automatically as a list of **steps**.
  It serves as an audit trail, can be exported as a table to document a pipeline, and can be
  replayed as an animation. Available via the `steps` property, `print_steps()`, `note()` for adding
  narration to the next step, `play()`, and `clear_steps()`. [Learn more](step-log.qmd).

Step player
: An animation with controls to step forward and back, play and pause, and jump to any frame. The
  player returned by `play()` rebuilds a graph from its **step log** one step at a time, with the
  code and narration of each step below the drawing; `plot_traversal()` and `record_traversal()`
  animate a search through a graph. Both produce a `StepPlayer`, which can be saved as a standalone
  HTML file. [Learn more](step-log.qmd#replaying-with-play).

Stochastic block model (SBM)
: A **random graph** model in which the nodes belong to groups and the probability of an edge
  depends only on the groups of its two endpoints. With high probabilities within groups, it
  generates communities; with other patterns, it generates core–periphery structure or
  disassortative groups. Fitting an SBM to a network is a principled form of **community
  detection**. Available via `generate_stochastic_block_model()` and
  `cmty_stochastic_block_model()`. See also **benchmark graph**. [Learn
  more](communities.qmd#a-fixed-number-of-groups).

Stored results
: EdgeCase's convention that a method that computes a value for every node, such as a **centrality**
  or a **community**, writes it to a node attribute named after the method (for example `pagerank`
  or `cmty_louvain`) and returns the graph, so that the results appear as columns of the **node
  table** and calls can be chained (see **chaining**). `attr_name=` stores the results under another
  name, and `return_dict=True` returns them as a dictionary keyed by **node ID** and leaves the
  graph unchanged. [Learn more](node-and-edge-data.qmd#attributes-written-by-algorithms).

Strongly connected component
: A maximal set of nodes of a **directed graph** in which every node can be reached from every other
  along directed edges. Available via `strongly_connected_components()`,
  `count_strongly_connected_components()`, and `is_strongly_connected()`. See also **weakly
  connected component** and **condensation**. [Learn more](connectivity.qmd#directed-graphs).

Structural equivalence
: The property of two nodes that have exactly the same **neighbors**, and so occupy the same
  position in the network. Approximate structural equivalence is measured by neighborhood
  **similarity**. [Learn more](similarity.qmd#structural-equivalence).

Subgraph
: A graph made of some of the nodes and edges of another. The subgraph *induced* by a set of nodes
  contains those nodes and every edge among them. Available via `subgraph()` for the subgraph
  induced by a list of nodes, `edge_subgraph()` for a set of edges, and `transform_to_subgraph_ws()`
  for the current **selection**. See also **ego network**. [Learn
  more](transforming.qmd#subgraphs).

Successor
: See **neighbor**.

Target
: See **source**.

Topological overlap
: A **similarity** of two nodes that combines whether they are linked with how many **neighbors**
  they share, normalized by the smaller of their **degrees**. In **co-expression networks**, the
  topological overlap matrix (TOM) is the basis for finding modules of genes. Available via
  `topological_overlap()`. [Learn more](network-biology.qmd#finding-modules).

Topological sort
: An ordering of the nodes of a **DAG** in which every edge points from an earlier node to a later
  one, such as an order in which tasks can be done that respects their prerequisites. A DAG usually
  has many. *Topological generations* group the nodes into stages that can proceed in parallel.
  Available via `topological_sort()`, `all_topological_sorts()`,
  `lexicographical_topological_sort()`, and `topological_generations()`. [Learn
  more](dags.qmd#ordering).

Trail
: A **walk** that doesn't repeat any edge, although it may revisit nodes. See also **Eulerian
  path**. Available via `count_trails()` and `enumerate_trails()`. [Learn more](paths.qmd#walks).

Transitive closure
: The graph that adds an edge from every node to every node it can reach, making all
  **reachability** explicit. Its opposite, the *transitive reduction*, removes every edge that is
  implied by a longer path, leaving the fewest edges with the same reachability, which gives the
  cleanest drawing of a **DAG** of dependencies. Available via `transitive_closure()` and
  `transitive_reduction()`. [Learn more](dags.qmd#closure-and-reduction).

Transitive reduction
: See **transitive closure**.

Transitivity
: The share of the connected triples of nodes (paths of two edges) that are closed into
  **triangles**, $3 \times \text{triangles} / \text{connected triples}$. It measures the tendency of
  the friends of a friend to be friends, over the whole graph. Also called the *global clustering
  coefficient*. Available via `transitivity()`. See also **clustering coefficient**. [Learn
  more](clustering-and-motifs.qmd#two-global-measures).

Traveling salesperson problem
: Finding the shortest route that visits every node once and returns to the start. It is hard to
  solve exactly for large graphs, so it is usually solved approximately. Available via
  `traveling_salesman()`. [Learn more](paths.qmd#the-traveling-salesperson-problem).

Traversal
: Visiting the nodes of a graph by following its edges, as in a **breadth-first search** or a
  **depth-first search**. In EdgeCase, the term also covers moving a **selection** along the edges:
  `trav_out()`, `trav_in()`, and `trav_both()` replace the selected nodes with their neighbors in
  the given direction, `trav_out_edge()` and `trav_in_edge()` move from nodes to edges, and
  `trav_out_until()` repeats until a condition holds. [Learn more](traversals.qmd).

Tree
: A connected graph without **cycles**, in which every pair of nodes is joined by exactly one path.
  A tree on $n$ nodes has $n - 1$ edges. A *rooted* tree has a distinguished root node, from which
  the others descend. Available via `is_tree()`, `add_balanced_tree()`, and
  `from_prufer_sequence()`. See also **forest**, **arborescence**, and **spanning tree**. [Learn
  more](dags.qmd#trees).

Treewidth
: A measure of how close a graph is to a **tree**: trees have treewidth 1, and denser graphs higher
  values. Many problems that are hard in general become easy on graphs of small treewidth. Available
  via `tree_decomposition()` and `chordal_graph_treewidth()`. See also **chordal graph**. [Learn
  more](coloring-matching.qmd#chordal-graphs-and-treewidth).

Triad
: A set of three nodes and the edges among them. A directed graph has sixteen types of triad, from
  three unlinked nodes to three nodes linked in both directions, and the *triad census* counts each
  type; it is a classic summary of social networks. Available via `triadic_census()`,
  `triad_type()`, and `triads_by_type()`. See also **motif**. [Learn
  more](clustering-and-motifs.qmd#triads-in-directed-graphs).

Triangle
: Three nodes that are all linked to each other, the smallest **clique** of more than two nodes.
  Triangles are the basis of the **clustering coefficient** and **transitivity**. Available via
  `count_triangles()` and `list_triangles()`. [Learn more](clustering-and-motifs.qmd#triangles).

type
: The kind of a node, such as `"person"` or `"place"`, stored in the `type` column of the **node
  table**. It is an **attribute** with a special role: **Cypher** queries read it as the node's
  label (as in `(p:person)`), and many methods can filter on it. It is set with the `type=` argument
  of `add_node()`, `add_nodes()`, and the **generators**. See also **rel**. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#types-and-attributes).

Undirected graph
: A graph whose edges have no direction, so that an edge from $a$ to $b$ is the same as one from $b$
  to $a$, as in friendships or collaborations. EdgeCase graphs are undirected unless created with
  `directed=True`, and an undirected edge still records which endpoint was given as its **source**
  and which as its **target**. See also **directed graph**. [Learn
  more](graph-model.qmd#directed-and-undirected-graphs).

Vertex
: See **node**.

Vertex cover
: A set of nodes that touches every edge, as when placing guards at intersections so that every
  street is watched. The complement of a vertex cover is an **independent set**. Available via
  `minimum_weighted_vertex_cover()`, `bipartite_vertex_cover()`, and `is_vertex_cover()`. [Learn
  more](coloring-matching.qmd#vertex-covers-and-independent-sets).

VoteRank
: A method for choosing a set of influential spreaders by rounds of voting: every node votes for its
  neighbors, the node with the most votes is chosen, and the neighbors of each chosen node lose
  voting power, so that the chosen nodes are spread across the network rather than clustered
  together. Available via `voterank()`. See also **influence maximization**. [Learn
  more](spreading.qmd#influential-spreaders).

Walk
: A sequence of nodes in which each is linked to the next, with nodes and edges allowed to repeat.
  The number of walks of length $k$ between two nodes is an entry of the $k$-th power of the
  **adjacency matrix**. Available via `count_walks()`. See also **path**, **trail**, and **random
  walk**. [Learn more](paths.qmd#walks).

Walktrap
: A **community detection** method based on **random walks**: short walks tend to stay within
  communities, so nodes are grouped by the similarity of where walks starting from them go.
  Available via `cmty_walktrap()`. [Learn more](communities.qmd#detection-algorithms).

Weakly connected component
: A maximal set of nodes of a **directed graph** that are connected when the edge directions are
  ignored. Available via `weakly_connected_components()`, `count_weakly_connected_components()`, and
  `is_weakly_connected()`. See also **strongly connected component**. [Learn
  more](connectivity.qmd#directed-graphs).

Weight
: A number attached to an edge, such as a distance, a cost, a capacity, or the strength of a tie,
  stored in the `weight` column of the **edge table**. Whether a larger weight means a stronger or a
  weaker connection depends on the method: **shortest paths** and **betweenness centrality** read
  weights as distances, while **PageRank** and **community detection** read them as strengths. See
  also **weighted graph**. [Learn more](graph-model.qmd#weighted-graphs).

Weighted graph
: A graph whose edges carry **weights**. A graph is weighted when it is created with
  `weighted=True`, and conversions such as `from_networkx()` and `from_numpy_array()` detect weights
  in the data. Methods that accept weights use them by default on a weighted graph. Available via
  `is_weighted()`. [Learn more](graph-model.qmd#weighted-graphs).

Wiener index
: The sum of the **distances** between all pairs of nodes, a classic descriptor of molecular graphs
  in chemistry. Available via `wiener_index()`, with `hyper_wiener_index()` for a variant.
  See also **mean distance**. [Learn more](paths.qmd#distance-based-indices).
